title: Patrick (c. 5th century)
hook: kidnapped from Britain as a boy, enslaved in Ireland, he returns freely to the people who held him

segments.voice: Yesterday, Augustine, the restless genius who heard a child sing take up and read. Your line was our heart is restless.

March seventeenth: green everything, parades, a river dyed green in Chicago. The Saint Patrick on the greeting cards comes with snakes, a shamrock and an Irish accent. Here's the surprise: he wasn't Irish. And nobody has to guess about him, because he left two short pieces of writing in his own words. The longer one he called his confession. It opens with him calling himself a sinner, very unlearned, the least of all the faithful. Not a legend. A man.
screen: `GREEN RIVERS AND GREETING CARDS.` → `HE WASN'T IRISH.` → `HIS OWN WORDS.`

segments.voice: Patrick grew up in Roman Britain. His father was a deacon, his grandfather a priest, and by his own account he didn't take any of it seriously. Then, when he was about sixteen, raiders from Ireland attacked his family's estate and carried him off with thousands of others. He was sold as a slave and spent six years herding animals on a cold hillside, and that's where his faith woke up. He writes that he prayed a hundred times in a day, and almost as many at night, in snow and frost and rain. One night he heard a voice in his sleep telling him a ship was ready. He walked, he says, about two hundred miles to the coast, talked his way onto a ship, and got home. Free. Safe. Family. Then the part that's hard to believe. He had a dream: a man came to him with letters, and he heard the voices of the Irish, calling him to come back and walk among them again. So he went back. Not as a slave this time, but as a bishop, to the island where he'd been owned, to the people who had held him. He spent the rest of his life there, baptizing thousands, facing threats and even arrest. And the famous bits? There were no snakes in Ireland to drive out, and he never mentions any. The shamrock explaining the Trinity is a lovely story, but it only shows up in writing many centuries later. The true story needs no help.
screen: `A BOY FROM ROMAN BRITAIN.` · `SIX YEARS A SLAVE.` · `THE VOICE OF THE IRISH.` · `NO SNAKES, LATE SHAMROCK.` · then, large: `HE WENT BACK.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who hurt you; you don't have to do anything as big as Patrick did, and you don't have to go back to anyone who isn't safe. Notice what happens in your body, breathe, and if you can, wish them one good thing, or, if you pray, pray for them by name. If no good wish comes today, let that be all right, and try another day.
Patrick. A British boy enslaved in Ireland, who escaped, and then freely went back to the people who had held him. Today's word.
Your line: he went back. Freely, to the people who had held him. That's day eighty-six.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Patrick on 17 March, a holy day in Ireland, and many pray the prayer known as Saint Patrick's Breastplate, though it was probably written later.

original.note: Latin: Patrick's name as he wrote it, meaning of noble or patrician rank.

trapdoor: what you thought: an Irish saint who drove out the snakes.
what it means: a British boy enslaved in Ireland, who escaped, then went back freely to the people who had held him.
what a scholar hears: two authentic texts, the Confessio and the Letter to Coroticus, in rough Latin. the snakes and shamrock come centuries later.

sources.work: Letter to the Soldiers of Coroticus

notes: All Patrick material is paraphrased from the Confessio (no public-domain translation on the approved list was used). Details: father Calpornius a deacon, grandfather Potitus a priest (§1); captured at nearly sixteen (§1); six years (§17); a hundred prayers a day and as many at night (§16); 200 miles to the ship (§17); the dream of Victoricus and the voice of the Irish (§23). Confirm.
Dates: Patrick's life is usually placed in the 5th century; exact dates are disputed.
'Facing threats and even arrest': Confessio §52 mentions being seized and put in chains. Confirm.
Snakes: no native snakes in post-glacial Ireland. Shamrock story first attested in the early 18th century. Confirm.
howItsDone mentions the Breastplate (Lorica) as 'probably written later'; confirm.
Chicago dyeing its river green for St. Patrick's Day is a well-known custom; confirm tone is fine.
